Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Margaret had been a social worker for forty years, helping survivors of domestic violence, but nothing prepared her for the abuse she endured from her own partner. The man she trusted began hitting her without warning. Now eighty, she lives alone, but the memories are fractured—snapshots of a door slamming, his hand mid-swing, the cold linoleum against her cheek. She cannot put them in order. Those fragments had become permanent triggers: the sound of any door opening could pull her back into that moment. And each time she recalls, grief floods her, overwhelming and fresh. That grief, combined with the feeling that her entire worldview had been shattered, drove her to try to erase the memory entirely. She would lie in bed, running through the details, seeking meaning that never came, but the search only deepened her conviction that people could not be trusted. That conviction meant that she felt endangered not just in specific situations but continuously, as if the threat lived inside her now.

The triggers were inescapable. A door opening in her apartment building would bring a snapshot rushing back. Because that image came so vividly, she began to see danger in other ordinary sounds—the clatter of a mailbox, the creak of a floorboard—as if the memory had sharpened her senses to every possible reminder. Being alone with any man made her skin crawl; she felt dirty, contaminated, as though the abuse had left a permanent stain. Her own son had become a source of dread. When he visited, she avoided being with him in the early evening, knowing that conversations often stirred nightmares. She also avoided napping, staying busy with crossword puzzles to push the thoughts away. Her sense of contamination made her avoid napping, as rest brought unwanted memories. But the meaning-seeking thoughts intruded anyway: Why had this happened to her? Her mistrust made her hypervigilant. She scanned every room for exits the moment she entered—the grocery store, the church hall, even her own living room. The constant watchfulness wore her out, yet she could not stop. She slept poorly, waking at the slightest noise. This exhaustion made her more reactive. A door slam in the hallway would make her jump, intensifying the trigger. In turn, her hypervigilance led her to avoid situations that might bring on nightmares—she went to bed very late, staying awake until too tired to dream. But her attempts to erase the memory paradoxically made the threat feel more present; she felt as though the abuse was following her. Living under that shadow of imminent threat, even a harmless knock at the door felt like an attack beginning, turning everyday sounds into triggers she could not ignore.

Her belief that people could not be trusted meant that any male presence became a trigger she could not avoid. And when a trigger occurred, she would immediately try to push the memory away—an attempt to regain control that only solidified her feeling of contamination. Each time she tried to make sense of the event, she concluded that the world was unsafe, which made her even more watchful. And the more watchful she became, the more she noticed men—their footsteps, their voices—turning ordinary encounters into triggers. Her efforts to erase the memory also made her hyperaware of potential reminders, so that a door click or a male voice became a trigger she could not ignore.

She had stopped attending family gatherings, claiming fatigue. Her son grew hurt and distant, but Margaret could not explain why she felt so unsafe around him. She came to therapy at his urging, after he found her crying uncontrollably when a door slammed at his house. She was terrified that she was losing her mind, that the past had invaded the present so completely that there was no escape. She hoped that someone could help her sort out the fractured images and quiet the grief that would not fade. What she feared most was that she would never feel clean again, that the stain of the abuse would follow her to the grave.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory directly causes any stimulus to become a trigger or increases sensitivity to triggers.
No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly causes any stimulus to become a trigger or intensifies the response to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the intrusive memory directly causes any stimulus to become a trigger or increases sensitivity to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly causes any stimulus to become a trigger or intensifies the response to triggers.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
